blocks.content: The story starts with a bank transfer at 11:58 PM.

You transfer ₹50,000 from your HDFC account to your friend's SBI account. Two completely separate databases. Two completely separate systems. Your HDFC balance needs to go down by ₹50,000. Your friend's SBI balance needs to go up by ₹50,000. Both need to happen. Or neither should happen. There is no acceptable universe where one happens without the other.
Now imagine the network dies at exactly the wrong moment after HDFC debited your account, but before SBI credited your friend's. ₹50,000 vanished from the world.
This is the distributed transaction problem. Two-Phase Commit is the protocol designed to solve it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027622-187701371.png
blocks.alt: Distributed bank transfer needs an atomic debit and credit or neither side happens

blocks.content: 1. Single database transactions

In a single database, transactions are simple. You wrap operations in BEGIN / COMMIT. If anything fails, you ROLLBACK. The database engine guarantees ACID either all operations commit together or none do.

The moment you have two databases, this guarantee evaporates. There's no single engine overseeing both. Each database can commit or fail independently. A crash between the two commits leaves you in an inconsistent state with no automatic recovery.

data:image/png;base64,

["The application starts a transfer of ₹50,000 from HDFC to SBI.","HDFC successfully deducts ₹50,000 and commits the transaction.","Before SBI can process the credit, the network fails.","SBI never receives the credit request.","As a result, ₹50,000 is debited from HDFC but never credited to SBI.","The system ends up in an inconsistent state.","Since the databases are independent, neither knows the other's final status.","Without a coordination mechanism like Two-Phase Commit (2PC), automatic recovery is not possible."]
items: The application starts a transfer of ₹50,000 from HDFC to SBI.
HDFC successfully deducts ₹50,000 and commits the transaction.
Before SBI can process the credit, the network fails.
SBI never receives the credit request.
As a result, ₹50,000 is debited from HDFC but never credited to SBI.
The system ends up in an inconsistent state.
Since the databases are independent, neither knows the other's final status.
Without a coordination mechanism like Two-Phase Commit (2PC), automatic recovery is not possible.

blocks.content: The core problem: you cannot atomically commit to two independent systems simultaneously. The network between them means there's always a gap a window where one side committed and the other hasn't. Two-Phase Commit is the protocol that minimises and manages that window.
The key players
Before explaining the protocol, establish who's involved:

Coordinator: the node that orchestrates the transaction. Typically the application server or a dedicated transaction manager. It initiates the transaction, talks to all participants, and makes the final commit/abort decision.

Participants: the databases, services, or resource managers involved in the transaction. They do the actual work. They each have a local write-ahead log and can vote on whether they're ready to commit.

data:image/png;base64,
2. Phase 1: Prepare (Voting phase)
The coordinator sends a PREPARE message to every participant. This is not a commit it's a question: "Can you guarantee that if I tell you to commit later, you will succeed?"
Each participant must now do real work:
["Execute the transaction locally","Acquire all necessary locks","Write the operations to its write-ahead log (WAL) durably, on disk","But do not commit yet"]
items: Write the operations to its write-ahead log (WAL) durably, on disk

blocks.content: If a participant can guarantee it will succeed, it votes YES. If anything is wrong constraint violation, disk full, lock timeout it votes NO.
The crucial guarantee: once a participant votes YES, it is irrevocably committed to committing if the coordinator says so. It has written to disk. It has the locks. It cannot change its mind.

data:image/png;base64,
After Phase 1, the coordinator collects all votes. If all participants voted YES, it proceeds to Phase 2 with a commit. If even one participant voted NO, it sends abort to everyone no exceptions.
3. Phase 2: Commit (or Abort)
Happy path all YES:

The coordinator writes COMMIT to its own log (this is the point of no return), then sends COMMIT to every participant. Each participant commits its local transaction, releases its locks, and acknowledges. The coordinator records completion.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305034284-803722853.png
blocks.alt: 2PC Phase 2 happy path: coordinator logs and sends COMMIT, participants ack

blocks.content: Unhappy path: any NO:
The coordinator sends ABORT to every participant. Participants roll back their local transactions, release locks, acknowledge. Clean slate.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305036333-986884740.png
blocks.alt: 2PC Phase 2 unhappy path: coordinator sends ABORT, participants roll back

blocks.content: 4. The failures: where 2PC gets hard
2PC works beautifully on paper. In a real distributed system, things fail. Understanding exactly what can go wrong and why is what separates a surface-level understanding from a deep one.
Failure 1: Participant crashes before voting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305037875-423736496.png
blocks.alt: Failure 1: participant crashes before voting, coordinator times out and aborts

blocks.content: A participant receives PREPARE, crashes before it can vote. The coordinator waits, times out, and since it never got a YES from everyone, it sends ABORT to all. Safe nobody committed anything yet.
Failure 2: Coordinator crashes after sending PREPARE but before Phase 2
blocks.text: Failure 2: Coordinator crashes after sending PREPARE but before Phase 2

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305039406-934764206.png
blocks.alt: Failure 2: coordinator crashes after PREPARE, participants blocked holding locks

blocks.content: This is the first nasty one. Participants voted YES. They're sitting there holding locks, waiting for the coordinator to tell them commit or abort. The coordinator is dead.

Participants are now blocked indefinitely. They cannot commit on their own (they don't know if everyone voted YES). They cannot abort on their own (they might be the only one, and the coordinator might have already told another participant to commit). They hold their locks. Nothing can proceed.
This is the blocking problem the fundamental weakness of 2PC. A coordinator failure after participants vote leaves the system stuck until the coordinator recovers.
Failure 3: Coordinator crashes after logging COMMIT but before sending COMMIT to all
blocks.text: Failure 3: Coordinator crashes after logging COMMIT but before sending COMMIT to all

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305041045-251430960.png
blocks.alt: Failure 3: coordinator crashes after logging COMMIT, resends on recovery

blocks.content: The coordinator wrote COMMIT to its own log. It sent COMMIT to Participant A. Then it crashed. Participant A committed. Participant B is still waiting.

When the coordinator recovers, it reads its log, sees it decided to commit, and resends COMMIT to everyone who hasn't acknowledged. Participant A gets a duplicate (idempotent it ignores it since it already committed). Participant B finally commits.
This is why the coordinator logs its decision before sending any commit messages. The log is the source of truth for recovery.
Failure 4: Participant crashes after voting YES but before receiving COMMIT
blocks.text: Failure 4: Participant crashes after voting YES but before receiving COMMIT

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305042551-601597811.png
blocks.alt: Failure 4: participant crashes after voting YES, recovers and queries coordinator

blocks.content: Participant voted YES, crashed. Coordinator sends COMMIT to everyone. The crashed participant misses it.

When the participant recovers, it reads its WAL, sees it wrote a prepared transaction, and contacts the coordinator to ask: "Did txn_123 commit or abort?" The coordinator tells it. The participant acts accordingly. This is called the recovery protocol.
5. The blocking problem

The scenario of coordinator failure after Phase 1 is not an edge case. It happens in production. And when it does, participants are stuck holding database locks until the coordinator recovers. Other transactions that want those rows are queued waiting. In a busy system, this is catastrophic.
This is the defining weakness of 2PC. It is called a blocking protocol because it can block indefinitely on coordinator failure. The only resolution is for the coordinator to come back online.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027809-311914118.png
blocks.alt: 2PC blocking problem: participants stuck holding locks, other transactions queued

blocks.content: The duration of the block depends on how fast your coordinator recovers. If you're using a single coordinator with no failover, this is however long it takes to restart the process potentially minutes. That means minutes of locked rows, queued transactions, and degraded service.
Mitigation strategies:

Make coordinators highly available run the coordinator on a cluster with automatic leader election (Raft-based). When the coordinator dies, a new one is elected in seconds, reads the log, and resumes the transaction.
Log the coordinator decision durably before sending anything the log is the recovery mechanism. Without it, even coordinator recovery can't determine what the decision was.

Use timeouts aggressively participants that have been waiting too long can contact other participants to see if anyone else received a commit or abort message. This is an optimisation but not a full solution.
6. 3PC the attempted fix
Three-Phase Commit was designed specifically to solve the blocking problem. It adds a third phase PRE-COMMIT between PREPARE and COMMIT.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305045759-104998460.png
blocks.alt: 3PC adds a PRE-COMMIT phase between PREPARE and COMMIT/ABORT

blocks.content: In 3PC, once the coordinator sees all YES votes, it sends PRE-COMMIT (not yet a final commit). Participants acknowledge. Now the coordinator sends COMMIT.
The key insight: if a participant knows everyone received PRE-COMMIT, it can unilaterally commit even if the coordinator dies because it knows the coordinator's decision was commit.
3PC sounds like the perfect fix. In practice, it's almost never used in production.

Why? It doesn't work under network partitions. If the network splits and participants can't talk to each other, they can make conflicting decisions some commit, some abort. 3PC assumes nodes can always talk to each other to detect the coordinator is dead.
In a real network partition, they can't. You can end up with split-brain some nodes committed, some aborted, and no way to reconcile.

This is actually an expression of the FLP impossibility result no distributed consensus protocol can be both safe and live in the presence of even a single process failure, under an asynchronous network model.
2PC chooses safety (it never commits inconsistently) at the cost of liveness (it can block). 3PC attempts to improve liveness but compromises safety under partitions.
7. Where 2PC is used in real systems
blocks.text: 7. Where 2PC is used in real systems

blocks.content: Databases with Distributed Transactions: When a transaction spans two databases, both databases first prepare the transaction. Once both confirm they are ready, the coordinator tells them to commit. If either database cannot prepare, both rollback.

Message Queue + Database: A service processes a Kafka message and writes data to a database. If the service crashes at the wrong time, the message may be processed again. 2PC ensures the database update and Kafka acknowledgment happen as one atomic operation.

Distributed Database Engines: In distributed databases, a transaction may involve multiple shards. 2PC ensures every shard commits the transaction together. This prevents some shards from updating while others do not.

Java EE / JTA: An application may need to update a database and send a message in the same transaction. JTA uses 2PC to coordinate both operations, ensuring they either succeed together or fail together.
The performance cost
2PC is expensive. Let's count the messages and roundtrips:
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305047377-853778800.png
blocks.alt: 2PC message cost for N=3 participants: 12 messages across 2 roundtrips

blocks.content: For N=3 participants: 12 messages, 2 network roundtrips minimum. If each roundtrip is 5ms (same data centre), that's 10ms of pure coordination overhead before any actual work is measured.
Across data centres (50ms roundtrip), that's 100ms of overhead. This is why distributed transactions are expensive and why engineers avoid them when possible.
Locks are held for the entire duration of both phases. High contention tables under 2PC become bottlenecks fast.
8. Why Modern Systems Avoid 2PC
Most modern distributed systems deliberately avoid 2PC and use other approaches. Knowing these is essential interviewers want to know you can reason about when to use 2PC and when to avoid it.

["Saga pattern. Break a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction for rollback. Order service commits, Payment service commits, Inventory service commits each independently. If inventory fails, a compensating saga sends a refund to Payment and cancels the Order. No global locks. Eventually consistent. Used heavily in microservices. The trade-off: business logic gets complex, you need to write compensating transactions, and the system is not isolated during the saga partial states are visible.
","Transactional outbox. Write to your database AND a special outbox table in the same local transaction. A separate process reads the outbox and publishes events to a message queue. Delivers exactly-once semantics without 2PC. Widely used. Debezium (CDC) can do the outbox reading via database change logs.
","Event sourcing. The truth is the event log. Services subscribe to events and update their own state. Eventual consistency no distributed transaction. Works well when strict consistency isn't needed immediately.
","Choose one authoritative database. The simplest approach if you can redesign your data model so that related data lives in the same database, you don't need 2PC at all. A local transaction with BEGIN / COMMIT solves everything with no coordination overhead. This is worth significant refactoring to achieve.
"]
items: Saga pattern. Break a distributed transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating transaction for rollback. Order service commits, Payment service commits, Inventory service commits each independently. If inventory fails, a compensating saga sends a refund to Payment and cancels the Order. No global locks. Eventually consistent. Used heavily in microservices. The trade-off: business logic gets complex, you need to write compensating transactions, and the system is not isolated during the saga partial states are visible.

Transactional outbox. Write to your database AND a special outbox table in the same local transaction. A separate process reads the outbox and publishes events to a message queue. Delivers exactly-once semantics without 2PC. Widely used. Debezium (CDC) can do the outbox reading via database change logs.

Event sourcing. The truth is the event log. Services subscribe to events and update their own state. Eventual consistency no distributed transaction. Works well when strict consistency isn't needed immediately.

Choose one authoritative database. The simplest approach if you can redesign your data model so that related data lives in the same database, you don't need 2PC at all. A local transaction with BEGIN / COMMIT solves everything with no coordination overhead. This is worth significant refactoring to achieve.

blocks.content: 9. HLD Interview Answer for 2PC

First, explain the problem. When a transaction involves multiple services or databases, we need to ensure that either all changes succeed or all changes fail. Otherwise, the system can become inconsistent.

Then introduce 2PC. In the first phase, the coordinator asks all participants if they are ready to commit. Each participant prepares the transaction and replies with YES or NO. In the second phase, if everyone says YES, the coordinator tells them to commit. If anyone says NO, it tells everyone to rollback.
Next, mention the main drawback. 2PC is a blocking protocol. If the coordinator crashes after participants have agreed, they must wait for it to recover before they can commit or rollback.
Then discuss modern alternatives. Most systems prefer the Saga pattern, transactional outbox, or keeping related data in a single database because they are simpler and more scalable.
Finally, connect it to the system. For highly critical systems like payments, 2PC can still be used with a highly available coordinator to minimize failures and keep data consistent.
